items.followUp: State three bases used to classify living organisms.

rubric.why: These are key aims of classification.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identification or naming organisms and 1 mark for grouping them by similarities and differences.

rubric.why: These are characteristics used as bases for classification.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each valid basis, up to 2 marks.

modelAnswer: Aims of classification: to identify organisms and arrange them into groups based on their similarities and differences.
It makes the study of the great variety of organisms easier and helps show their relationships.
Basis of classification includes cellular organization, body structure, mode of nutrition, reproduction and evolutionary relationships.

items.followUp: Define aerobic respiration and distinguish it from anaerobic respiration.

rubric.why: Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen and involves incomplete breakdown of glucose.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it occurs without oxygen and 1 mark for incomplete breakdown of glucose or release of energy.

rubric.why: The two common types produce different end products.
rubric.description: Explains the types of anaerobic respiration.
rubric.how: Award marks for describing alcoholic fermentation in yeast, which produces ethanol and carbon dioxide, and lactic acid fermentation in muscle cells or bacteria, which produces lactic acid.

modelAnswer: Anaerobic respiration is the incomplete breakdown of glucose to release energy in the absence of oxygen.
In alcoholic fermentation, yeast converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide, releasing energy.
In lactic acid fermentation, glucose is converted into lactic acid, releasing energy; this occurs in muscle cells when oxygen is insufficient and in some bacteria.

items.followUp: Describe four functions of the human liver.

rubric.why: The liver produces bile, which helps in the digestion of fats.
rubric.description: States that the liver produces bile.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying bile production.

rubric.why: The liver has important roles in storage, detoxification and metabolism.
rubric.description: Describes other functions of the liver.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each valid function, such as storing glucose as glycogen, detoxifying harmful substances, converting ammonia to urea, or making plasma proteins.

modelAnswer: The liver is the largest gland in the human body and produces bile, which helps in the digestion of fats.
It stores excess glucose as glycogen and releases glucose when needed.
It detoxifies harmful substances in the blood.
It converts ammonia into urea and makes important plasma proteins.

items.followUp: Compare the structure and functions of red and white blood cells.

rubric.why: These are characteristic features and the main transport role of red blood cells.
rubric.how: Award marks for red colour/haemoglobin, biconcave shape or absence of a nucleus in mature cells, and transport of oxygen.

rubric.why: White blood cells are nucleated and protect the body against infection.
rubric.how: Award marks for noting that white blood cells have a nucleus and defend the body by phagocytosis or antibody production.

rubric.why: A further correct comparison or fact completes the note.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid additional fact, such as red blood cells being formed in bone marrow or living about 120 days, or white blood cells being fewer than red blood cells.

modelAnswer: Red blood cells (RBCs) contain haemoglobin, which gives them their red colour.
Mature human RBCs are biconcave and lack a nucleus; they transport oxygen in the blood.
White blood cells (WBCs) have a nucleus and do not contain haemoglobin.
WBCs protect the body against infection by engulfing pathogens or by producing antibodies.
RBCs are far more numerous than WBCs; RBCs are formed in bone marrow and live for about 120 days.

items.followUp: What is a community? Give one example.

rubric.why: A population consists of members of the same species.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that its members belong to the same species.

rubric.why: A population occupies an area at a particular time; an example demonstrates the definition.
rubric.description: States the location/time condition or gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct area-and-time condition or a suitable example.

modelAnswer: A population is a group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time.
For example, all the frogs living in a pond form a population.

items.followUp: Write the scientific names of the cat and wheat plant.

rubric.why: This is the scientific name used for the frog in school-level classification.
rubric.description: Gives the scientific name of frog.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct binomial name.

rubric.why: This is a scientific name for mustard used in school-level classification.
rubric.description: Gives the scientific name of mustard plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct binomial name.

modelAnswer: Frog: Rana tigrina.
Mustard plant: Brassica campestris.

items.followUp: Give one quantitative and one qualitative observation about a leaf.

rubric.why: Quantitative observations are expressed numerically or measured.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is numerical or measurable; a suitable numerical example also earns the mark.

rubric.why: Qualitative observations describe qualities or characteristics rather than amounts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is descriptive or non-numerical; a suitable descriptive example also earns the mark.

modelAnswer: A quantitative observation is numerical or measurable; for example, a leaf is 8 cm long.
A qualitative observation describes a quality without using numbers; for example, the leaf is green.

items.followUp: Why are tables and graphs used when presenting biological data?

rubric.why: Summarization organizes collected results into a concise form.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that results or data are organized or arranged, often in tables or graphs.

rubric.why: A summary makes results easier to interpret and draw conclusions from.
rubric.description: States the purpose of summarizing results.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that organized results make data easier to understand, compare, identify patterns in, or draw conclusions from.

modelAnswer: Summarization of results is the organization and presentation of collected data in a concise, meaningful form, often using tables or graphs.
It makes the results easier to understand and compare, and helps reveal patterns or support conclusions.
